Welcome! Your goal is to move all your checkers around the board and bear them off before your opponent. Let\'s practice each skill!
This is the starting position. Your orange checkers move toward your home board (bottom-right). Let\'s roll!
Tap the dice button to roll — or shake your phone! Each die lets you move one checker by that many points.
Now drag one of your checkers to a green-highlighted destination. Tap a checker to see where it can go.
See that lone white checker? Move your checker onto it to hit it! A single opponent checker is vulnerable.
Your checker is on the bar. You must re-enter it onto the board before moving any other checker. Roll and enter!
All your checkers are in your home board! Now bear them off by rolling and moving past position 24. Bear off to win!
Excellent! You\'ve mastered the basics. Enjoy playing for real!

Nacre checkers, walnut dice, and pearl ripple — three layers of one ocean.
Nacre is broken under light to release its hidden colours — pink, green, and gold that shift with angle. These pieces are cut from shells no longer found in the Gulf.
Copper checkers, copper dice, and madder smoke — from the coppersmiths\' bazaar.

Isfahan\'s coppersmiths have hammered in one alley for three generations. Copper\'s colour changes with heat — from fresh orange to old brown — and these pieces were quenched at exactly the moment the colour was best.
Checkers, dice, and turquoise spark — all from the mines of Neyshabur.
Turquoise does not sit in veins but in pockets, each one its own shade. These pieces take their colour from three different pockets — no two boards lit the same way will show the same blue.
The deep blue — checkers, dice, and the night they leave behind.

Lapis lazuli has been ground for paint since before paint had a name. These pieces are not painted — they are the stone itself, shaped and polished. The colour is not applied: it is the material, and it does not fade.
The golden colour of Yazd — checkers, dice, and the golden haze they leave.

More than a hundred thousand filaments go into a kilogram of saffron. The colour of these pieces is exactly that: the dried thread, pressed into something that holds its shape. The hue shifts in different light — richer at dusk, paler at noon.
Banded stone cut into checkers, dice, and the ember of landing — the most popular bundle.

The caravan road from Yemen to Persia carried spices one way and agate the other. Each band in the stone is a year of slow geology, and the craftsman cutting it does not choose which bands show. Every pair of checkers is therefore unique.
Haft-rang board, Isfahan frame, and Isfahan sound — a city in one box.

Haft-rang is a ceramic tradition whose colours are fired at eight hundred degrees so they will never fade. The Isfahan frame is taken from the same geometric knotwork that repeats across Khaju Bridge. The sound rises from the same square.
Pateh board, caravan frame, and caravan sound — from the Safavid road.

Pateh from Kerman is embroidered on silk with wool thread — patterns that require the reader to know where to look. This board was under one family\'s hands in Kerman for three months. The sound is from the khans along the road from Kerman to Isfahan.
Four sounds from four cities — Neyshabur, Shiraz, Tabriz, and Yazd.
Each city has its own resonance. This bundle gives four sound sets: Neyshabur pottery, Shiraz bazaar, Tabriz workshops, and Yazd badgirs — for anyone who wants each match to feel different.
Three boards — khatam, mina, and nacre — from three different workshops.

Khatam needs a month of assembly for a surface the size of your palm. Mina is enamel fired on copper at eight hundred degrees. Nacre is cut from shells of oysters no longer found in the Gulf. These three boards are from the workshops that still know how.
Zari board, Yazd frame, and Yazd sound — from the silk weavers.

Zari is woven from silver or gold thread — fabric that carries light inside it. The board in this set is drawn from the Yazd weavings that have supplied court robes for centuries. The sound is from the city\'s tall badgirs.
Checkers and dice cast in the only metal that does not age.
Gold does not corrode and gold does not age. The pieces in this set are not gilded — there is no base metal underneath — and in a century of playing they will look exactly as they do now.
Board, checkers, and dice — all from the filigree workshops of Tabriz.

Tabriz silversmiths flatten wire to the width of a hair and bend it cold, without solder, into shapes that support their own weight. The board, checkers, and dice in this set all come from the same workshop on the same street — and nothing on the shelf costs more.
24-karat Persian gold with a royal pattern
Clear crystal dice with a light shimmer
Legendary dice with a dragon motif
International rules: the starter plays the opening dice. Gammon 2, backgammon 3 points.
Turkish style: the opening winner rolls again (doubles possible). Mars 2 points, no triple win.
Greek style (first game of Tavli): the opening winner rolls again. Gammon 2 points, no triple win.
Greek style: all 15 start on the opposite corner. Landing on a lone checker pins it until you leave. Pin the last checker on its start (the mother) to win double.
Greek running game: both run the same way from opposite corners, no hitting, one checker holds a point. Your lead checker must pass the opponent\'s start before any other moves.
Greek match: Portes, then Plakoto, then Fevga, repeating until someone reaches the target score.
Both sides run the same way from opposite heads. No hitting: one checker holds a point. One checker leaves the head per turn. Mars 2 points.
No turns to grade in this game.
Win the previous chapter to open this one.
Where every player starts: a quiet game and a patient opponent.
Three games against the regulars, where speed matters less than steadiness.
Tavla, played fast: the starter rolls again and mars is worth two.
Portes, the first game of Tavli, a cousin of the game you know.
Plakoto: no hitting here, only pinning — and the mother decides everything.
Fevga: one checker leads the way until it passes the opponent\'s start.
Long Nardy: no hitting, one checker per turn off the head, blocks decide the race.
A full Tavli match: Portes, Plakoto and Fevga against the strongest opponent.
American style: all checkers start off the board and enter like from the bar. A 1-2 roll adds a double of your choice and another roll. The loser pays a point for every checker still on the board.
Acey-deucey, the sailors\' game: every checker starts off the board and a 1-2 changes everything.

The whole road is behind you. Play any chapter again whenever you like.
Turned from a single block. The set everyone learns on.
Warm, close-grained, and heavier in the hand than it looks.
Ebony inlaid in the marquetry of Isfahan, star within star.
The inside of the shell, which changes colour as the board turns.
The blue Persia is known for, from the mines above Neyshabur.
Banded carnelian, cut and polished like a seal stone.
A set for a table nobody plays on. Play on it anyway.
The pair every table starts with. Light, loud, honest.
Nearly black, and heavy enough to land where you throw it.
Veined with the matrix it grew in. No two faces alike.
Banded through, so every roll shows a different cut of the stone.
They roll slower. Everyone watches them anyway.
For the player whose doubles keep arriving.
For the one who builds the prime and never lets it open.
Winning is enough for most people.
Where nothing is hit, only pinned — and the mother decides.
Held only while it is true.
The marquetry workshops, where a star is built from a thousand slivers of ebony and bone.
Above the town, the mines that gave the colour its name. The best stone never leaves the province.
What the divers brought up, and what the workshops on the quay made of it.
Agate came north with the caravans, already banded, already worth more than the camel that carried it.
When the season closes, this set is withdrawn and is not sold again.
Ten thousand slivers to the square span.

Khatam is brass wire, ebony and camel bone drawn into rods no thicker than a bristle, bundled into a hexagon and sliced across. Every slice is one star. A board this size is a month of slices laid one beside the next.
The dice land in a haze off the kiln.
Isfahan\'s enamellers fire their blue three times over, and every firing leaves a fine powder on the bench. The dice pick it up and carry it.

Twenty columns standing in the air and twenty standing in the water beneath them. Nobody has ever counted forty in one place. This one is not for sale at any price: it is given for finishing the Isfahan chapter.
Raised from the back, eight points.
A chaser works the sheet from behind, lifting the metal with a few hundred small blows, then turns it and sinks the lines from the front.
Mina kari is enamel laid into chased copper and taken back to the kiln for every colour. Blue goes in first because it survives the most heat.
Struck light, the colour of the mine.
Hit turquoise matrix with steel and it throws a short blue spark. The miners used to find the seam that way in the dark.
The seam at Neyshabur has been worked for longer than anyone has been keeping count. Given for finishing the Neyshabur chapter.
Set the way a ring is set.
The stone is cut flat, bedded on a rim of metal, and the rim pushed over its edge until it holds without glue.
The inside of a shell, sawn flat.
Nacre is the lining an oyster lays down in sheets thinner than paper. Sawn across, those sheets split light, which is why no two points on this board are quite the same colour.
Drop anything into still water in the shallows and the ring reaches the boat before the sound does.
A diver\'s rope was held by one other man, and that was the whole of the safety arrangement. Given for finishing the harbour chapter.
Cut from one piece, not inlaid.
Big enough a shell that the whole ring comes out of a single curve of it, which is rarer than the stone in it.
Cut down into the wood, not laid on it.
Monabbat is carving: the pattern is what is left after the ground is taken away. Nothing is added, so nothing can lift.
Hold banded agate to a lamp and the bands go through it one after another, like looking down a road at dusk.
Stones came up the road in sacks and went back as seals with someone\'s name cut backwards into them. Given for finishing the caravan chapter.
Cut so the bands run across the ring rather than around it, which wastes most of the stone and is the only way the pattern reads.
Play for it. It is not sold.
Buy it, or play for it

Mosaic is cut from seven glazes and assembled; haft-rang is painted in seven glazes and fired once. The colours creep into each other at the edges in the kiln, and that bleed is how you tell one from the other at a glance.
Blue with its own gold in it.
Lapis is not dyed. The gold specks through it are pyrite, sitting in the stone where it formed, which is why no two pieces in a set match.
Cut across the vein, not along it.
Cut along the vein and every face is a different blue. Cut across it and the six faces finally agree.
The pyrite comes off the stone as it is worked and hangs in the lamplight for a long time afterwards.
Given for finishing the Shiraz chapter, and by no other route.
Cut flat and bedded low, because lapis chips if the rim is pushed hard.
Holding two points in the opponent\'s home and waiting. It loses badly when it loses, which is the price of the way it wins.
Pateh is wool sewn onto wool until no ground is left showing. The whole cloth is covered by a single needle, and a good one is a winter\'s work.
Kerman\'s coppersmiths do not lacquer their work. It goes brown, then almost black, and is brought back with a lemon.
Warm in the hand before the throw.
Copper takes the heat of a hand faster than bone or stone, which is either a superstition or the reason people prefer them.
Madder root gives a red that goes brown before it ever goes pink, which is how an old pateh is dated.
Given for finishing the Kerman chapter, and by no other route.
The wool is stretched over a copper ring and stitched down the back where the join will not be seen.
A point held to the end.
One point in the opponent\'s home that is never given up, however long the game goes against you.
Filigree is silver drawn out to the thickness of a hair and bent into a pattern with nothing behind it. The pattern is the structure; take one wire out and the rest sags.
Mostly air. A full set weighs less than a single walnut piece, and players either love that or cannot stand it.
Hollow filigree would not roll true, so these are wound over bone and weigh what a die should weigh.
Light off a hundred wires at once.
A filigree piece has no flat face to catch the light, so it catches all of it at every angle instead.
Given for finishing the Tabriz chapter, and by no other route.
The only frame here with nothing behind it. What you see through the gaps is whatever is behind the screen.
Attacking the opponent\'s home board before it is closed, on the theory that a game decided early is a game that cannot turn.
Termeh is woven so slowly that a weaver counts progress in finger-widths. The pattern is in the weave, not printed on it, so the back is the front in reverse.
The colour is not a dye. It is what the stone does when the sun is behind it, which is why a set indoors and the same set outdoors look like two sets.
Cut from the same block as the checkers, so the pair and the set were the same stone before anybody shaped them.
The hour before dark in Yazd, when the walls give back everything they took all day.
Given for finishing the Yazd chapter, and by no other route.
Turned from a single piece so the bands run unbroken all the way round, which wastes most of the block.
The last stretch, where the dice stop being luck and start being arithmetic.
Wood on wood, under a dome.
Recorded the way a tea house sounds: a piece set down hard, and the room giving it back a half-second later.
Turquoise on a hard board rings rather than knocks.
Shell, and water under the floor.
Quieter than the rest. Shell does not carry.
No room to give anything back, so every piece lands once and that is all.
A fired glaze has a note in it. Two pieces set down together are almost a chord, which is either lovely or maddening.
The wool takes the edge off every knock, which is the point of playing on a pateh at all.
Filigree has almost no mass, so it clicks and stops.
Open above, walls close on four sides: one knock and four answers.
Seven glazes painted together and fired once, so the colours bleed into one another in the kiln.
Wool sewn onto wool until no ground shows, by one needle, over a winter.
Silver drawn to the thickness of a hair and bent into a pattern that stands up with nothing behind it.
Woven a finger\'s width at a time, the pattern in the weave rather than printed on it.
